full_prose_under_review.title: Schedule II Partial Fills and the Massachusetts 30-Day Ceiling
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Choosing the pathway, the clock, the record and the actor
learning_objectives: Distinguish a prohibited refill from a lawful remainder of a partial fill.
Choose the federal remainder clock by identifying which partial-fill pathway the facts trigger.
Apply the Massachusetts 30-day issue-date ceiling on top of whichever federal clock the pathway supplies.
Apply the Massachusetts five-day limit using the trigger the regulation actually states.
State what each actor must specify or record in each pathway.

orientation.text: A Schedule II prescription cannot be refilled. That single sentence causes most of the confusion in this area, because a partial fill looks like a refill from the counter: the patient comes back and leaves with more drug. The difference is that a refill is a fresh authorisation to dispense the full quantity again, while the remainder of a partial fill is the unfilled balance of the one quantity the prescriber already authorised. Nothing is created; something already authorised is completed. Getting that distinction right is what lets the rest of the area make sense.

Federal law then supplies three separate partial-fill pathways, and each carries its own clock. Where the pharmacy simply could not supply the full quantity, the remainder may be filled within 72 hours of the first partial filling, after which the prescriber must be notified and no further quantity may go out without a new prescription. Where the patient or the prescriber asked for a partial fill, the remainder runs to 30 days after the prescription was written -- except that an emergency oral prescription collapses that to 72 hours from issue. Where the patient is in a long-term care facility or has a documented terminal illness, partial filling may continue for up to 60 days from issue unless the medication is discontinued sooner. The first question on any partial-fill fact pattern is therefore never 'how long', it is 'which pathway', because the pathway picks the clock.

Massachusetts then puts a ceiling over all of it. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) provides without qualification that a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance. There is no long-term care or terminal-illness carve-out from that sentence. So the federal 60-day figure, which is a real and correctly stated federal outer limit, cannot be worked in Massachusetts past day 30: counting the day after issue as day one, as 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs, on day 31 there is no longer a valid prescription for the pathway to operate on. A federal outer limit is a ceiling on federal authority. It is never a grant of state validity, and the 60-day answer belongs only to a question that asks what federal law alone permits.

Massachusetts also has its own partial-fill scheme, and it appears twice with two different triggers. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request, keeps the remainder at the same pharmacy, requires a patient-record notation, closes the remainder at 30 days from issue, and imposes a five-day limit on the INITIAL partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2). 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same five-day limit but triggers it off something a pharmacist can actually see: whether the prescriber's address ON THE PRESCRIPTION is outside the Commonwealth, counted in calendar days. The regulation is the operational form of the statute's rule, and it is the one that decides the question at the counter.

Finally the records, which are where the actors separate. On the stock-shortage pathway the pharmacist notes the quantity supplied. On the request-based pathway the practitioner's part is conditional: a practitioner who wants the prescription partially filled specifies the quantity for each partial filling, and that specification then caps what the patient side may later ask for; where the request comes instead from the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney, nothing is required of the prescriber first. The pharmacist's notation follows whoever asked: the quantity dispensed where the prescriber asked on the prescription; 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill', with the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials, where the prescriber authorized the partial fill in a later consultation; and who requested it and on what date, with the quantity dispensed, where the patient side asked. On the long-term care and terminal-illness pathway the notation is not clerical at all: a partially filled prescription that does not carry 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' is deemed by the regulation to have been filled in violation of the Act. Massachusetts adds a patient-record notation, made by the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee, and it puts a separate duty on the prescribing practitioner: a Schedule II opioid prescription must carry on its face the notation that the patient may request less than the full quantity.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts written oxycodone prescription for an LTCF resident is issued on 1 March and partially filled on 5 March under the federal long-term care pathway. On 12 April the facility asks for a further partial quantity. The prescription has not been discontinued and quantity remains authorised. Federal law would still allow it. May you dispense?
steps: Confirm the federal pathway is genuinely open. 12 April is day 42 from issue, inside the 60-day outer limit, and the medication has not been discontinued, so federal law does not stop you.
Now apply the Massachusetts ceiling. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidates a written or electronic Schedule II prescription 30 days after the date of issuance, without qualification.

Count the days as 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs, with the day after issue as day one: 31 March is day 30, the last day inside the 30 days, and from 1 April the prescription is invalid. That was eleven days before the request, which fell on day 42.

Ask what the federal 60-day figure actually is. It is an outer limit on that federal pathway, not a grant of Massachusetts validity, so it cannot revive a prescription the state has already invalidated.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The prescription is dead in Massachusetts and a further partial dispensing would be made on an invalid prescription. The error this invites is answering 60 days because the question mentions an LTCF resident; 60 days is the right answer only where the question asks what federal law alone permits.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a Schedule II prescription written by a Rhode Island prescriber whose address is printed on the prescription, issued six days ago, and asks for only part of the quantity. Your colleague says the five-day limit does not apply because nobody has established which statutory subsection the prescription came in under.
steps: Read the regulation rather than the statute. 105 CMR 721.055(A) attaches the five-day limit where the prescription was issued by a prescriber from a location other than the Commonwealth, as indicated by the address of the prescriber on the prescription.
That test is satisfied on its face here: the address printed on the prescription is out of state. No subsection adjudication is required.
Count in calendar days from the prescription issue date, which is what the regulation specifies. Six days is outside the limit.

Do not treat the limit as touching only the partial fill. Unless the Rhode Island prescriber also holds a registration under chapter 94C, the prescription was not issued under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(a), and it can be filled in Massachusetts only under s. 18(d), for a nonnarcotic Schedule II drug, or s. 18(d1/2), for a narcotic one from a practitioner registered in Maine or a contiguous state such as Rhode Island. Each of those subsections authorizes filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days.
So the 30-day Massachusetts validity period is not there to fall back on. On day six a prescription that depends on s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2) cannot be filled at all, in full or in part.
worked_examples.resolution: No fill of any kind can be made on these facts unless the prescriber also holds a Massachusetts registration. Even then, 105 CMR 721.055(A) bars the partial fill the patient asked for, because it keys off the out-of-state address on the prescription and six calendar days have passed; only a full fill within the 30-day validity period would remain. The colleague's test is the statute's; the regulation supplies an address-based trigger that the pharmacist can apply from the face of the prescription, and it is the operative one at the counter.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber writes a Schedule II prescription for 60 tablets and specifies on its face that it is to be partially filled in three dispensings of 20. After the first 20 are dispensed, the patient telephones and asks for 30 next time because they are going away. Your technician says a patient may request any quantity they like.
steps: Confirm the request route is valid. A patient may request a partial fill in person, in writing if signed, or by telephone, so the telephone call is not the problem.
Check whether the practitioner has already specified quantities. Here they specified 20 per filling on the face of the prescription under 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(3).
Apply the cap. Where the practitioner has requested partial filling in that way, the patient may not request a partial filling in an amount greater than the practitioner specified.
Keep the running total in view: across all partial fillings the total dispensed may not exceed the total quantity prescribed.
Record the request properly: the patient requested a partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed.
worked_examples.resolution: You may dispense up to 20, not 30. Going to 30 would need the prescriber to change the specification. The technician's rule is right, within the total prescribed, for a prescription the practitioner left unspecified, and wrong for this one.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Three federal partial-fill pathways, three clocks: stock shortage ______; requested partial fill ______; LTCF or terminal illness ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 72 hours from the first partial filling; 30 days from when the prescription was written (72 hours from issue if it was an emergency oral prescription); up to 60 days from the issue date.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why can a Massachusetts LTCF partial fill not run to 60 days?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidates a written or electronic Schedule II prescription 30 days after issuance with no LTCF or terminal-illness carve-out, and a federal outer limit is not a grant of state validity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the Massachusetts five-day partial-fill limit applies only once you have established that the prescription was filled under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2).
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 105 CMR 721.055(A) triggers it off the prescriber's address as it appears on the prescription, counted in calendar days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A partially filled LTCF prescription does not carry the words 'LTCF patient' or 'terminally ill'. What follows?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The regulation deems it to have been filled in violation of the Act.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What four things must be recorded for EACH partial filling on the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The date of the partial filling, the quantity dispensed, the remaining quantity authorised to be dispensed, and the identification of the dispensing pharmacist.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where the practitioner has already specified per-fill quantities, may the patient request a larger partial fill?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. A patient, a minor's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's named caregiver may not request more than the practitioner specified.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a patient may ask for a partial fill of a Schedule II prescription only if the practitioner specified per-fill quantities on it.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The per-fill specification is owed only where the practitioner wants the prescription partially filled. The patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney may ask without it, and in Massachusetts the pharmacist must then dispense the lesser quantity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A prescriber specified on a Schedule II prescription, when issuing it, that it be dispensed in two partial fillings. What does the pharmacist note at the first one?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The quantity dispensed, on the face of the written prescription or in the electronic record, and the pharmacy keeps the dispensing record. 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' is for a partial fill the prescriber authorized later in a consultation, and the requester-and-date entry is for a patient-side request.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In Massachusetts, is dispensing a lesser quantity on patient request permitted or required?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Required. The pharmacist shall dispense the lesser quantity if the patient requests it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where must the Schedule II opioid partial-fill notation appear, and who puts it there?
retrieval_prompts.answer: On the prescription itself: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) makes it part of what the prescribing practitioner must include when issuing a Schedule II opioid prescription. It is a different thing from the patient-record notation the pharmacist or designee makes at each partial dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: On federal law alone, may a second pharmacy dispense the remaining portion of a partially filled Schedule II prescription?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 21 CFR 1306.08(e) transfers an electronic prescription only for its initial dispensing and 21 CFR 1306.25 moves only Schedule III-V prescription information for refills; DEA has stated that no DEA regulation permits a partially filled prescription to be transferred for the remaining portion. Massachusetts reaches the same result expressly in s. 18(d3/4).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule II prescription from a Rhode Island prescriber who holds no Massachusetts registration is presented six days after issue. May it be filled in full instead of in part?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Such a prescription is fillable in Massachusetts only under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), and each authorizes filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days.

quick_review.text: A Schedule II prescription may not be refilled; dispensing a lawful unfilled remainder of a partial fill is not a refill.

Federal law supplies three partial-fill pathways with three different remainder clocks: 72 hours when the pharmacy could not supply the full quantity, 30 days from the writing date when the patient or prescriber requested the partial fill, and up to 60 days from issue for an LTCF resident or a terminally ill patient.

In Massachusetts a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a), so no federal pathway can be worked past day 30 on that prescription.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request, keeps the remaining portion at the same pharmacy, requires a patient-record notation of the partial fill and quantity, and requires the remaining portion to be filled not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date. Federal law gives no route to move the remaining portion to another pharmacy either.

105 CMR 721.055(A) states the five-day initial partial-fill limit with an address-based trigger: it applies where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth, counted in calendar days from issue.

A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner who is not registered under M.G.L. c. 94C can be filled in Massachusetts only under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), and only if it was issued within the preceding five days, whether the fill is full or partial.

Every federal partial fill carries a notation duty of its own. A practitioner who wants a request-based partial fill specifies the per-fill quantities, and a patient-side request then cannot exceed them; a request by the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney needs no prior specification. On the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway a partially filled prescription lacking the 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' notation is deemed filled in violation of the Act.

The prescribing practitioner must include on a Massachusetts prescription for a Schedule II opioid a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity.

decision_logic.condition: The original Schedule II quantity was fully dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Do not process an additional dispensing as a refill; require a new lawful prescription unless a distinct pathway applies.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy could not supply the full Schedule II quantity.
decision_logic.action: Note the quantity supplied on the prescription record, then use the 72-hour remainder rule; past 72 hours notify the prescriber and obtain a new prescription for any further quantity.

decision_logic.condition: The patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney, or the prescriber requested a partial fill of a written or electronic Schedule II prescription, and state law does not prohibit it.
decision_logic.action: If the practitioner specified per-fill quantities, keep any patient-side request within them; make the notation that fits the requester (the quantity dispensed for a request made on the prescription, 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' with the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials for one made in consultation, or the requester and the date of the request with the quantity dispensed for a patient-side request); keep the dispensing record; and complete any remainder no later than 30 days after the prescription was written.

decision_logic.condition: The patient or prescriber requested a partial fill of an emergency oral Schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Complete any remainder no later than 72 hours after the prescription was issued; the ordinary 30-day request-based period does not reach an emergency oral prescription.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule II prescription is for an LTCF resident or a patient with a documented terminal illness.
decision_logic.action: Record 'LTCF patient' or 'terminally ill' on the prescription before partially filling it, contact the practitioner first if terminal status is uncertain, and log the date, quantity dispensed, remaining quantity authorised and dispensing pharmacist for each partial filling.

decision_logic.condition: The prescriber's address printed on a Schedule II prescription is outside Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: The prescription must be presented for initial partial fill not later than five calendar days after its issue date.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner who is not registered under M.G.L. c. 94C is presented more than five days after issue.
decision_logic.action: Do not fill it at all, in full or in part: s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) authorize filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days.

decision_logic.condition: The federal pathway you selected would allow a further partial dispensing more than 30 days after the Massachusetts written or electronic Schedule II prescription was issued.
decision_logic.action: Stop. The prescription is already invalid in Massachusetts under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a); the federal outer limit is a ceiling on federal authority and does not extend Massachusetts validity.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts patient requests a lesser quantity of a Schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Dispense the lesser quantity, note the partial fill and quantity in the patient record accessible to the prescriber on request, keep any remainder at the same pharmacy, and fill it not later than 30 days after the issue date.

decision_logic.condition: The patient asks a different pharmacy to dispense the remaining portion of a partially filled Schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Decline: under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) only the pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion, and no federal transfer pathway moves a partially filled prescription to a second pharmacy.

ma_vs_federal.text: 21 CFR 1306.13(c) allows LTCF and terminal-illness Schedule II partial fills for up to 60 days from issue, but M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidates the written or electronic prescription 30 days after issuance. Both apply, so in Massachusetts the working outer limit is 30 days and the federal 60-day figure answers only a question about federal law alone.

Federal request-based partial filling is permissive, and among its conditions are that the partial fill is not prohibited by State law and that the prescription is written and filled in accordance with State law; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) goes further and makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request, and adds a patient-record notation and a 30-day issue-date deadline of its own for the remaining portion.

Both sovereigns keep the remaining portion at the pharmacy that made the partial fill. Massachusetts says so expressly in s. 18(d3/4); federally no transfer pathway reaches a partially filled prescription, because 21 CFR 1306.08(e) is for initial dispensing and 21 CFR 1306.25 for Schedule III-V refills, and DEA has stated that no DEA regulation permits the remaining portion to be transferred.
Partial-fill notation is not a Massachusetts-only duty: 21 CFR 1306.13(a) and (b)(5) impose federal notation and dispensing-record duties that run alongside the Massachusetts patient-record notation.

exceptions.text: The 72-hour remainder rule is tied to the pharmacy's inability to supply the full quantity and is not a substitute for the request-based pathway.

The request-based 30-day remainder period carries its own emergency-oral exception: the remainder of a partially filled emergency oral Schedule II prescription must be filled no later than 72 hours after the prescription is issued.
The 60-day LTCF and terminal-illness period is an outer limit on that federal pathway, not an extension of any state validity period, and it ends earlier if the medication is discontinued.

The five-day initial partial-dispensing limit in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) reaches only a prescription filled under subsection (d) or (d1/2) -- respectively a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner and a narcotic Schedule II prescription from a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth -- and not every patient-requested partial fill. Those two subsections also authorize filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days, so a prescription that depends on them cannot be filled at all after that point, in full or in part; their other conditions belong to the out-of-state pathway.

Where the practitioner has specified per-fill quantities in advance, a patient-side request may not exceed them, and no pathway permits the total across all partial fillings to exceed the total quantity prescribed.
The day-counting rule in 247 CMR 9.04(10) is one of the requirements 247 CMR 9.04(15) disapplies at institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

forms_records.text: On the stock-shortage pathway the pharmacist notes the quantity supplied on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic prescription record.

On the request-based pathway the notation follows whoever asked. Where the prescriber asked for partial filling on the prescription when issuing it, having specified the quantity for each partial filling, the pharmacist notes the quantity dispensed on the face of the written prescription or in the pharmacy's electronic records, in the record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic prescription record. Where the prescriber authorized a later partial fill in a consultation, the pharmacist notes 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill', the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials. Where the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney asked, no prior specification is needed, and the pharmacist notes that that person requested the partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed.

Each request-based partial filling also generates a dispensing record carrying the date, the name or initials of the person who dispensed, and the elements 21 CFR 1306.22(c) requires for Schedule III and IV refills; for an electronic prescription that information must be linked to the electronic prescription record.

On the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway the pharmacist records 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' on the prescription itself, and for each partial filling records the date, the quantity dispensed, the remaining quantity authorised and the dispensing pharmacist's identification.

Massachusetts adds a notation of each partial dispensing and its quantity in the pharmacy patient record, made by the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and accessible to the prescribing practitioner on request, whether the dispensing is the initial partial fill or the remaining portion.

The prescribing practitioner must include on a Massachusetts prescription for a Schedule II opioid the notation under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity. It is part of the prescription's content, separate from the pharmacist's patient-record notation.

role_duties.duty: Identify the factual trigger for the partial fill before selecting any deadline, because the three federal pathways carry three different clocks.

Where the practitioner wants a Schedule II prescription partially filled, specify the quantity to be dispensed in each partial filling on the prescription when it is signed, or authorize a later partial fill after consultation with a pharmacist, and keep the total within the quantity prescribed. A partial fill requested by the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney requires nothing of the prescriber first.
Include on every Massachusetts Schedule II opioid prescription the notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity.

Make the partial-fill notation that fits the requester and keep the dispensing record for each request-based partial filling: the quantity dispensed where the prescriber asked on the prescription, the 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' entry after a consultation, and the requester and date, with the quantity, for a patient-side request.
Check the Massachusetts issue-date ceiling before dispensing any remainder, since a federal pathway that is still open may sit on a prescription Massachusetts has already invalidated.
Dispense the lesser quantity when a Massachusetts patient requests a partial fill of a Schedule II prescription; that dispensing is mandatory rather than discretionary.

Contact the practitioner before partially filling where it is unclear whether the patient may be classified as terminally ill; the responsibility to assure the substance is for a terminally ill patient is shared with the prescriber.

common_traps.text: Calling every later Schedule II dispensing a refill erases the lawful partial-fill remainder distinction.
Choosing 72 hours whenever a Schedule II prescription is partial ignores who requested the partial fill and why.
Carrying the federal 60-day figure into a Massachusetts scenario dispenses a Schedule II drug on a prescription that M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidated on day 31.
Reading the Massachusetts patient-requested partial fill as an option the pharmacist may decline turns a mandatory duty into a permission.
Looking for the statutory subsection before applying the five-day limit misses that the regulation triggers it off the prescriber's address printed on the prescription.
Treating the LTCF or terminal-illness notation as clerical overlooks that a partially filled prescription without it is deemed filled in violation of the Act.
Assuming a patient may request any partial quantity ignores the cap a practitioner's advance specification imposes.
Turning away a patient's partial-fill request because the prescriber specified no per-fill quantities treats a condition of the prescriber's own request as a condition of the patient's.

Assuming the pharmacist adds the Schedule II opioid partial-fill notation, or that it lives only in the pharmacy record, misses that M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) makes it part of the prescription the practitioner issues.

Reading the out-of-state five-day figure as a partial-fill deadline only, and filling in full later, overlooks that s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) authorize filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding five days.
Calling the same-pharmacy remainder rule a Massachusetts-only restriction misses that no federal transfer pathway reaches a partially filled prescription either.

authority.name: Schedule II prescriptions may not be refilled

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Federal law prohibits refilling a Schedule II prescription; additional dispensing requires a new lawful prescription or a permitted remainder of a partial fill.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Schedule II partial fill caused by pharmacy inability

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: When a Schedule II prescription is partially filled because the pharmacy cannot supply the full quantity, the remaining portion must generally be supplied within 72 hours or the pharmacist must notify the prescriber and obtain a new prescription for further quantity.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Schedule II prescription may be partially filled at the patient or prescriber request when state law permits, with the remaining portion dispensed no later than 30 days after the prescription was written unless a shorter applicable limit controls.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Federal law permits Schedule II prescriptions for LTCF residents or terminally ill patients to be partially filled under a special documentation framework for up to 60 days from issue unless the prescription is discontinued sooner.

authority.name: Request-based partial filling, conditions and records

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.13(a) the stock-shortage partial fill is permissible only if the pharmacist MAKES A NOTATION OF THE QUANTITY SUPPLIED on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic prescription record. The REQUEST-BASED pathway in 1306.13(b) allocates duties to both actors. Its general conditions in (b)(1) are conjunctive: the partial fill is not prohibited by State law; the prescription is written and filled in accordance with the Act, the chapter and State law; the partial fill is requested by the PATIENT, by one acting on the patient's behalf (a parent or legal guardian of a minor, or a caregiver of an adult patient named in a medical power of attorney), or by the PRACTITIONER who wrote the prescription; and THE TOTAL QUANTITY DISPENSED IN ALL PARTIAL FILLINGS DOES NOT EXCEED THE TOTAL QUANTITY PRESCRIBED. Under (b)(3), a practitioner who wants the prescription partially filled MUST SPECIFY THE QUANTITY TO BE DISPENSED IN EACH PARTIAL FILLING on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic record; after consultation with a pharmacist the practitioner may authorize a partial fill at a later date, but the prescription must still be filled not later than 30 days after it was written, or 72 hours for an emergency oral prescription. Under (b)(4) a request may be made in person, in writing if signed by the requester, or by telephone; and WHERE THE PRACTITIONER HAS ALREADY SPECIFIED QUANTITIES UNDER (b)(3), the patient, guardian or named caregiver MAY NOT REQUEST A PARTIAL FILLING GREATER THAN THE AMOUNT THE PRACTITIONER SPECIFIED. Under (b)(5) the pharmacist's notation differs by requester: a practitioner request made in consultation is noted as 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' with the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials, while a patient, guardian or caregiver request is noted as that named person having requested the partial fill on a stated date, together with the quantity dispensed. Every request-based partial filling also generates a dispensing record carrying the date, the name or initials of the dispenser, and the other elements 21 CFR 1306.22(c) requires for Schedule III and IV refills; for electronic prescriptions that information must be LINKED to the electronic prescription record.
exceptions: The stock-shortage notation under 1306.13(a) is only the quantity supplied; the fuller request-based notations belong to 1306.13(b)(5).
A consultation-authorized partial fill adds the 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' notation that a partial fill specified on the face of the prescription does not require.
Where the practitioner has specified per-fill quantities, a patient-side request cannot exceed them.
The remaining-portion period is 30 days from writing, except 72 hours where the prescription was an emergency oral one.

authority.name: Partial filling for LTCF residents and terminally ill patients

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.13(c) the pharmacist MUST RECORD ON THE PRESCRIPTION whether the patient is 'terminally ill' or an 'LTCF patient', and A PARTIALLY FILLED PRESCRIPTION THAT DOES NOT CARRY THAT NOTATION SHALL BE DEEMED TO HAVE BEEN FILLED IN VIOLATION OF THE ACT. If there is any question whether a patient may be classified as terminally ill the pharmacist must CONTACT THE PRACTITIONER BEFORE partially filling, and pharmacist and prescribing practitioner carry a CORRESPONDING RESPONSIBILITY to assure the substance is for a terminally ill patient. For EACH partial filling the dispensing pharmacist shall record, on the back of the prescription or on another appropriate uniformly maintained and readily retrievable record, the DATE of the partial filling, the QUANTITY DISPENSED, the REMAINING QUANTITY AUTHORIZED to be dispensed, and the IDENTIFICATION OF THE DISPENSING PHARMACIST. The total dispensed in all partial fillings must not exceed the total quantity prescribed.
exceptions: The notation duty is not a formality: 21 CFR 1306.13(c) deems a partially filled prescription without it filled in violation of the Act.
Where terminal-illness status is uncertain the practitioner must be contacted before the partial fill, not after it.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Massachusetts written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after its issue date.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws
authority.section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4), read with s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) a pharmacist filling a Schedule II prescription SHALL, if requested by the patient, dispense a lesser quantity; ONLY THE SAME PHARMACY that dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion; a notation of the partial fill and quantity goes in the patient record, accessible to the prescriber on request; and the remaining portion MUST BE FILLED NOT LATER THAN 30 DAYS AFTER THE PRESCRIPTION ISSUE DATE. The separate FIVE-DAY limit on the INITIAL partial dispensing applies only to a prescription FILLED PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (d) OR (d1/2) -- respectively a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription issued by an out-of-state practitioner, and a narcotic Schedule II prescription issued by a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth.

authority.name: Contents of prescription written by practitioner

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) any prescription issued by a practitioner for an OPIOID substance contained in Schedule II SHALL INCLUDE A NOTATION on the prescription that the patient may fill it, upon request, in compliance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) in an amount NOT TO EXCEED THE FULL PRESCRIBED QUANTITY. The notation is a prescription-content duty on the prescriber that accompanies the patient's statutory right to receive a lesser quantity on request.
exceptions: The notation duty reaches prescriptions for opioid substances in Schedule II; it is not a general notation requirement for every controlled-substance prescription.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the Massachusetts patient-requested partial fill as a duty: a pharmacist filling a Prescription for a schedule II controlled substance SHALL, IF REQUESTED BY THE PATIENT, dispense the substance in a lesser quantity than indicated, pursuant to M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4). It then supplies the operative trigger for the five-day limit: IF THE PRESCRIPTION WAS ISSUED BY A PRESCRIBER FROM A LOCATION OTHER THAN THE COMMONWEALTH, AS INDICATED BY THE ADDRESS OF THE PRESCRIBER ON THE PRESCRIPTION, the Prescription MUST BE PRESENTED FOR INITIAL PARTIAL FILL NOT LATER THAN FIVE CALENDAR DAYS after the Prescription issue date. That is a different test from the statute's 'filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2)': the pharmacist reads the address on the face of the prescription rather than adjudicating which statutory subsection the prescription travelled under, and the count is expressly in CALENDAR days. Under 721.055(B) the remaining portion may be filled on patient request provided only the same pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity dispenses it and it is filled not later than 30 days after the issue date, and under 721.055(C) the pharmacist or designee makes a notation in the patient record, accessible to the prescribing practitioner on request, of the partial fill and the quantity dispensed.
exceptions: The five-calendar-day limit attaches only where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth.

authority.name: Partial filling at the request of the prescribing practitioner, and how the pharmacy records it

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(3), where a practitioner issues a prescription for a Schedule II controlled substance and wants the prescription to be partially filled, the practitioner must specify the quantity to be dispensed in each partial filling on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the record for an electronic prescription. That information, except an authorization for partial filling at a later date, must be included on the prescription, with the other information 21 CFR 1306.05 requires, at the time the practitioner signs it, or, for an emergency oral prescription, communicated by the prescribing practitioner to the pharmacist during the oral communication. After consultation with a pharmacist, a practitioner may authorize a partial fill at a date after the prescription was initially issued, but the prescription must be filled not later than 30 days after the date on which it is written, except that the remaining portions of a partially filled emergency oral prescription, if filled, must be filled not later than 72 hours after it is issued. Under 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(5)(i), upon partially filling a prescription at the request of the prescribing practitioner, as requested when the prescriber issued the prescription, the pharmacist must make a notation of the quantity dispensed on the face of the written prescription or in the pharmacy's electronic records, in the written record or the pharmacy's electronic records of the emergency oral prescription, or in the record of the electronic prescription. When the pharmacist partially fills a prescription after the prescriber has conveyed the request in a consultation with a pharmacist, the pharmacist must note 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill', the name of the practitioner, the date and time of the discussion, and the pharmacist's initials. For each such partial filling, whether requested by the prescriber on the prescription or after consultation with the pharmacist, the pharmacy must maintain a record of dispensing that includes the date of each dispensing, the name or initials of the individual who dispensed the substance, and all other information 21 CFR 1306.22(c) requires for Schedule III and IV prescription refills; for electronic prescriptions, the quantity dispensed, the date dispensed and the dispenser must be linked to each electronic controlled substance prescription record.
exceptions: The per-fill specification is owed only where the practitioner wants the prescription partially filled; a request by the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney is made under 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(4) and does not depend on it.

The 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' notation belongs to a partial fill the prescriber authorized in a later consultation with a pharmacist, not to one specified on the prescription when it was issued.

authority.name: Transfer of an electronic controlled-substance prescription for initial dispensing
Transfer between pharmacies of prescription information for Schedules III, IV, and V controlled substances for refill purposes
DEA final rule, Transfer of Electronic Prescriptions for Schedules II-V Controlled Substances Between Pharmacies for Initial Filling, preamble response to comments on partial fills

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 21 CFR 1306.08(e) permits the transfer of an electronic prescription for a Schedule II-V controlled substance between retail pharmacies only for initial dispensing, upon request from the patient, on a one-time basis only. 21 CFR 1306.25(a) permits the transfer of original prescription information only for a controlled substance listed in Schedule III, IV or V, and only for the purpose of refill dispensing. In the preamble to the final rule that added the initial-dispensing transfer (88 FR 48365, July 27, 2023), DEA answered comments asking whether a pharmacy may partially fill a controlled substance prescription and transfer the remainder to another pharmacy: existing regulations permit the transfer of Schedule III-V prescriptions for refill dispensing only, the final rule permits the transfer of electronic Schedule II-V prescriptions between DEA-registered retail pharmacies for initial dispensing, and no DEA regulation permits a partially-filled controlled substance prescription to be transferred from one DEA-registered pharmacy to another for dispensing of the remaining portion of the prescription. Federal law therefore gives a second pharmacy no route to dispense the remaining portion of a partially filled Schedule II prescription.
exceptions: 21 CFR 1306.08(e) still allows a one-time transfer, at the patient's request, of an electronic Schedule II-V prescription for its initial dispensing.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(a) a prescription for a controlled substance may be issued only by a practitioner who is authorized to prescribe controlled substances and registered pursuant to chapter 94C. Section 18(d) provides that a prescription for a nonnarcotic substance in Schedule II may also be issued by a practitioner who is licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice and registered in another state where the practitioner resides or practices, if required, and registered under federal law to write prescriptions. Section 18(d1/2), except as provided in s. 18A, provides the same for a narcotic substance in Schedule II where the practitioner is so licensed and registered in Maine or in a state contiguous with the commonwealth. Each subsection is only for the purpose of authorizing the filling, within the commonwealth, of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days, and does not authorize the practitioner to possess, administer or dispense controlled substances under s. 9 or to practice within the commonwealth. A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner who is not registered under chapter 94C is therefore fillable in Massachusetts only under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), and only if it was issued within the preceding five days, whether the fill is full or partial.
exceptions: A practitioner who is authorized to prescribe controlled substances and registered under chapter 94C issues under s. 18(a), and the five-day filling window of s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) does not govern that prescription.
The narcotic route in s. 18(d1/2) reaches only practitioners registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth, and is subject to s. 18A.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: In order to determine whether a prescription is WITHIN DATE, a pharmacist shall count the DAY AFTER the prescription was written as DAY ONE. The issue date itself is not counted, so a period measured in days runs from the following day.

Under 247 CMR 9.04(15), the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(4), (5), (6), (9), (10), (12), (13) and (14) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. The excluded requirements include the counting rule in 9.04(10), under which a pharmacist deciding whether a prescription is within date counts the day after the prescription was written as day one; the Schedule VI rule in 9.04(12), under which a Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue and may not be refilled after one year; the Schedule V rule in 9.04(13), under which a Schedule V prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after issue or refilled more than five times; and the refill record in 9.04(6), under which a pharmacist refilling a Schedule III-VI prescription records the date of dispensing, the amount dispensed and his or her initials.

full_prose_under_review.title: Federal and Massachusetts Rule Interaction
learning_objectives: Solve a federal-state interaction by identifying the same actor, event, and prescription pathway under both sources.
Avoid selecting a familiar federal limit before checking Massachusetts conditions that also govern the transaction.

orientation.text: Two sovereigns reach the same dispensing at the same instant, and neither one announces where the other stops mattering. Federal controlled-substance regulation mostly draws an outer boundary: it describes the most a registrant may do without violating federal law, and it does not confer authority to do that thing where the pharmacy actually stands. 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1) says so in its own text. A Schedule II prescription may be partially filled at a patient's or practitioner's request only if all four of its conditions are met: the partial fill is not prohibited by State law; the prescription is written and filled in accordance with the Act, the federal regulations and State law; the request comes from the patient, a parent or legal guardian of a minor patient, a caregiver of an adult patient named in a medical power of attorney, or the practitioner who wrote the prescription; and the total dispensed across all partial fillings does not exceed the total prescribed. Two of the four point at the state. Read the first exactly: it asks for an absence of state prohibition, not for affirmative state permission, so a jurisdiction that says nothing does not block the partial fill. The second reaches further than it looks, because a prescription that falls short of what State law requires of it has not been written in accordance with State law, and the federal permission is unavailable until that defect is cured.

Now put one patient-requested Schedule II partial fill in front of both sources and take it part by part, because the relationship changes from part to part. Whether the pharmacist dispenses the lesser quantity is a state duty inside a federal permission: federal law permits the partial fill, while under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) a pharmacist SHALL dispense the lesser quantity if the patient requests it. Where the remaining portion may be dispensed is the same answer under both sovereigns: s. 18(d3/4) allows only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity to dispense it, and federal law gives a second pharmacy no route either, because 21 CFR 1306.08(e) transfers an electronic prescription only for its initial dispensing, 21 CFR 1306.25 moves only Schedule III-V prescription information for refills, and DEA has stated that no DEA regulation permits a partially filled prescription to be transferred for its remaining portion. What record the dispensing leaves is cumulative: the pharmacist notes that the patient requested the partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed, and the pharmacy keeps a federal dispensing record for each partial filling, while Massachusetts separately requires a notation of the partial fill and the quantity in the patient's record, accessible to the prescriber on request. Neither record stands in for the other. By when the remaining portion must go out has two matching answers: not later than 30 days after the prescription was written, or 72 hours after issue for an emergency oral prescription, federally, and not later than 30 days after the issue date in Massachusetts.

Other parts of the same transaction are governed by Massachusetts alone. The federal remainder clock in 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) times only the remaining portions of a requested partial fill; it does not time the first dispensing. Massachusetts does: under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance, so the first dispensing of an in-state prescription, partial or full, has to fall within those 30 days, counting the day after the prescription was written as day one as 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs. Section 18(d3/4) adds a shorter limit on the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), the two out-of-state routes: not more than 5 days after the issue date. 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same five-day limit, counted in calendar days, wherever the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth. And M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) requires any prescription a practitioner issues for an opioid substance in Schedule II to include a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in compliance with s. 18(d3/4), in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity. That duty falls on the prescriber as a matter of what the prescription must contain. It is a different duty from the patient-record notation made at each partial dispensing, and running the two together puts the obligation on the wrong actor. Silence on the federal side is not an argument that any of these points is unregulated.

A different interaction is harder to see, because nothing about it looks like a conflict. Federal law and Massachusetts law each carry a five-refill limit and a six-month limit measured from the issue date, and the two numbers are identical. The scopes are not. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) is addressed to a controlled substance listed in Schedule III or IV: no such prescription may be filled or refilled more than six months after the date it was issued, and none authorised to be refilled may be refilled more than five times. 247 CMR 9.04(13) states the same two limits for Schedule V, and for Schedule V alone. Massachusetts then narrows its own provision by facility rather than by schedule: 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. Storing 'five refills, six months' as a single remembered fact loses all of this. The figure is correct in two places and controlling in neither until the schedule -- and, in Massachusetts, the facility -- is matched to the transaction in front of you.

The working method that survives all of these patterns is the same one. Fix the schedule, the actor, the triggering event, the pathway and the facility before opening any rule. Then take each part of the transaction in turn -- whether it may happen, who must do it, where, by when, and what record it leaves -- and apply every rule, from either sovereign, whose scope actually reaches that part. A federal figure that answers one part, as the 30-day remainder clock answers by when, says nothing about another part, such as where the remainder may be dispensed. Finally, read the stem for which sovereign it is asking about: a stem that names a place rather than a body of law is asking about both.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a Massachusetts-issued Schedule II opioid prescription for 60 tablets on the day it was written and asks for 20 tablets now. You dispense 20. Eighteen days later the patient asks a different pharmacy in the same chain for the remaining 40. That pharmacist reads 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2), sees that the remaining portion may be filled up to 30 days after the prescription was written, and prepares to dispense.
steps: Define the transaction before opening any rule: Schedule II, a Massachusetts-issued prescription filled in Massachusetts, a partial fill triggered by the patient's own request, and a remaining portion sought on day 18 at a pharmacy that did not make the partial fill.

Read what the federal clock answers. 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) says by when a remaining portion, if filled, must be filled, and day 18 is inside the 30 days from writing. It does not say where; the clock is satisfied, but that is all it settles.

Ask how the prescription could reach the second pharmacy under federal law. 21 CFR 1306.08(e) allows a one-time transfer of an electronic prescription only for its initial dispensing, and this one has already been partly dispensed; 21 CFR 1306.25 moves only Schedule III-V prescription information for refills. DEA has stated that no DEA regulation permits a partially filled prescription to be transferred for its remaining portion. Belonging to the same chain does not make the second store the pharmacy that made the partial fill.
Massachusetts reaches the same answer in terms: under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity shall dispense the remaining portion.

Test the 5-day figure before discarding it. It governs the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), the out-of-state routes, and this prescription is on neither. The first dispensing, on the day of writing, was well inside the 30 days of s. 23(a) in any event.

Close the record when the first pharmacy dispenses the remainder within the 30 days: the federal notation that the patient requested the partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed, the federal dispensing record, and the Massachusetts notation in the patient's record.
worked_examples.resolution: The second pharmacy may not dispense the remaining 40 tablets; the pharmacy that dispensed the first 20 may, within the 30 days. Both sovereigns give that answer. The error the scenario invites is treating a federal clock that answers 'by when' as if it also answered 'where', and then calling the same-pharmacy result a Massachusetts addition, when on a question about federal law alone the answer is the same.

worked_examples.scenario: A Schedule V controlled-substance prescription written seven months ago, still showing two unused refills, is presented at a Massachusetts community pharmacy. A colleague reasons that 21 CFR 1306.22(a) states its six-month limit for Schedules III and IV only, that no federal six-month rule names Schedule V, and that the remaining refills may therefore be dispensed.
steps: The colleague has read the federal provision correctly. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) is addressed to a controlled substance listed in Schedule III or IV, and its six-month and five-refill limits are stated for those schedules.

Reading it correctly is not the same as finishing. A federal rule that does not reach Schedule V leaves the question open rather than resolving it in the pharmacy's favour, so the next step is to ask what Massachusetts says about the schedule in front of you.

247 CMR 9.04(13) supplies exactly the limits the federal provision does not: a Schedule V prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after the date it was issued, and may not be refilled more than five times.

Seven months have run from the issue date. The two unused refill authorisations do not survive that limit, because the six-month clock runs from issue rather than from the first or the most recent dispensing.

Confirm the facility before applying the Massachusetts provision. 247 CMR 9.04(15) removes 247 CMR 9.04(13) from institutional sterile compounding pharmacies; a community pharmacy is not one, so the provision reaches this dispensing.
worked_examples.resolution: No refill may be dispensed, and a new prescription is needed. The error the scenario invites is treating the absence of a federal rule as a permission, when the schedule the federal provision does not reach is precisely the one Massachusetts covers itself. The number the colleague needed was the same number he had already found, in the other sovereign's rule.

worked_examples.scenario: A Schedule II opioid prescription presented at your Massachusetts pharmacy carries no notation about partial filling. The patient asks you to dispense half of the prescribed quantity now. A technician tells you that because the prescription does not carry the notation the statute requires, the patient has no right to ask for a lesser quantity and you should dispense the full amount.
steps: Separate the two Massachusetts provisions the technician has run together. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) requires any prescription a practitioner issues for an opioid substance contained in Schedule II to include a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in compliance with s. 18(d3/4), in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity. That is a prescription-content duty owed by the prescribing practitioner.

The patient's entitlement sits elsewhere, in s. 18(d3/4): a pharmacist filling a Schedule II prescription shall, if requested by the patient, dispense the substance in a lesser quantity than the prescription indicates. It is not stated as conditional on the notation, so the prescriber's omission does not take it away, and dispensing the full amount over her request is not an answer either.

Now apply all four federal conditions, not three. Besides the patient's request, a total within the quantity prescribed and the absence of a state prohibition, 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1) requires the prescription to be written and filled in accordance with State law. A Schedule II opioid prescription issued without the notation s. 22(c) requires was not written in accordance with State law, so the federal permission for a partial fill is not yet available on this prescription as it stands.
Cure the defect at its source. Contact the prescriber so that the prescription carries the required notation, then dispense the lesser quantity the patient asked for.

Then complete both sets of steps: the federal notation that the patient requested the partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed, and the dispensing record; the Massachusetts notation in the patient's record, accessible to the prescriber on request; and the remaining portion kept at this pharmacy, to be filled not later than 30 days after the issue date.
worked_examples.resolution: Neither of the technician's conclusions holds. The missing notation does not cancel the patient's right to a lesser quantity, and it does not license a full fill over her request. What it does is leave the prescription short of State law, which keeps the federal partial-fill permission out of reach until the prescriber supplies the notation; then the lesser quantity is dispensed. The error the scenario invites is converting a prescriber's content duty into a precondition of the patient's own right, while overlooking that federal law makes compliance with State law a condition of the partial fill.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient brings a Massachusetts-issued electronic Schedule II prescription that has never been dispensed and asks for half the quantity now. Counting the day after it was written as day one, today is day 33. A colleague points out that the federal clock in 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) times only the remaining portions, which have not even begun, and says the partial fill can go ahead.
steps: Check what the federal rule actually times. 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) limits when the remaining portions, if filled, must be filled; it does not time the first dispensing, so the colleague has read that provision correctly.
Then ask what Massachusetts says about the prescription itself. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance.
Count as 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs, with the day after the prescription was written as day one. Day 33 is past day 30, so there is no longer a valid prescription to fill in part or in full.
Note why the federal remainder rule cannot help: a remaining portion presupposes a lawful first dispensing, and none can now be made. Only a new prescription starts the process again.
worked_examples.resolution: No quantity may be dispensed. The error the scenario invites is treating a federal clock that does not time the first dispensing as permission to make it, when a Massachusetts limit governs that part of the transaction by itself.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Fill in the blank: the first condition 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1) states for a patient-requested Schedule II partial fill is that the partial fill is ______. Why does the exact wording matter?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Not prohibited by State law. The condition is stated as an absence of state prohibition rather than as a requirement of affirmative state permission, so a jurisdiction that says nothing does not block the partial fill; restating it the other way reverses the default.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Fill in the blank: besides the absence of a state prohibition, the other State-law condition in 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1) is that the prescription is ______. Why does it matter when a Massachusetts Schedule II opioid prescription lacks the s. 22(c) notation?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Written and filled in accordance with the Act, the federal regulations and State law. A prescription missing a notation State law requires was not written in accordance with State law, so the federal partial-fill permission is not available until the prescriber cures the omission; the patient's s. 18(d3/4) right itself is not lost.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A patient partially filled a Schedule II prescription at pharmacy A and wants the remaining portion from pharmacy B on day 18. Which sovereign keeps the remainder at pharmacy A?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Both. Massachusetts says expressly in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) that only the pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion. Federally no transfer pathway reaches a partially filled prescription: 21 CFR 1306.08(e) is for initial dispensing, 21 CFR 1306.25 for Schedule III-V refills, and DEA has stated that no DEA regulation permits the remaining portion to be transferred.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What records does one patient-requested Schedule II partial fill leave in a Massachusetts pharmacy?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The federal notation that the patient (or the parent, guardian or named caregiver) requested the partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed; a federal dispensing record with the date, the dispenser's name or initials and the 21 CFR 1306.22(c) information; and the Massachusetts notation in the patient's record, accessible to the prescriber on request. They are cumulative.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) limit when the first partial dispensing of a Schedule II prescription must happen, and what limits it in Massachusetts?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No; it times only the remaining portions. In Massachusetts the prescription is invalid 30 days after issuance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a), counting the day after it was written as day one under 247 CMR 9.04(10), and a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2) must have its initial partial dispensing not more than 5 days after the issue date.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Fill in the blanks: the 5-day limit in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) governs the ______ dispensing, and only where the prescription is filled pursuant to ______; the remaining portion must be filled not later than ______ after the prescription issue date.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Initial partial; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2); 30 days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the five-refill and six-month limits in 21 CFR 1306.22(a) are the source of the Massachusetts Schedule V refill limits.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) states those limits for Schedules III and IV. The identical Schedule V limits are Massachusetts law, at 247 CMR 9.04(13); matching numbers do not make the two provisions one rule.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which Massachusetts facility category does 247 CMR 9.04(13) not reach, and where is that stated?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(13), among others, do not apply to them, so a matching federal number does not remove the facility-scope inquiry.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which sovereign requires a Schedule II opioid prescription to carry a notation about the patient's partial-fill right, and on which actor does that duty fall?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Massachusetts, at M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c), and the duty falls on the prescribing practitioner as a matter of prescription content. It is not the pharmacy patient-record notation that s. 18(d3/4) separately requires at each partial dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: where the s. 22(c) notation is missing from a Schedule II opioid prescription, the patient loses the right to request a lesser quantity.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The notation is the prescriber's duty, and the patient's right to a lesser quantity on request in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) is not expressed as conditional on it. The omission still matters: the prescription falls short of State law, so the prescriber should be contacted to cure it before the partial fill.

quick_review.text: Federal request-based Schedule II partial filling requires all four conditions of 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1): the partial fill is not prohibited by State law; the prescription is written and filled in accordance with federal and State law; the request comes from the patient, a parent or legal guardian of a minor patient, a caregiver named in an adult patient's medical power of attorney, or the prescribing practitioner; and the total dispensed does not exceed the total prescribed.

In Massachusetts the pharmacist must dispense the lesser quantity when the patient asks, only the same pharmacy may dispense the remaining portion, each partial dispensing is noted in the patient's record, and the remaining portion must be filled not later than 30 days after the issue date.
Keeping the remaining portion at the pharmacy that made the partial fill is not a Massachusetts-only rule: no federal transfer pathway moves a partially filled prescription to another pharmacy.
A Massachusetts patient-requested partial fill generates both the federal notation and dispensing record and the Massachusetts patient-record notation.

A Massachusetts written or electronic Schedule II prescription is invalid 30 days after issuance, counting the day after it was written as day one, so its first dispensing must fall within that period even though the federal remainder clock does not time it.

Federal Schedule III-IV and Massachusetts Schedule V refill rules each use a five-refill limit and a six-month issue-date limit within their respective scope; Massachusetts excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(13).

decision_logic.action: Define the drug schedule, actor, trigger, pathway and facility first; then take each part of the transaction (whether, who, where, by when, what record) and apply every rule whose scope reaches it.

decision_logic.condition: Federal law allows a patient-requested Schedule II partial fill that State law does not prohibit.
decision_logic.action: Continue to the Massachusetts conditions instead of stopping at federal permission, and confirm the prescription was written in accordance with State law.

decision_logic.condition: The remaining portion of a partially filled Schedule II prescription is sought at a pharmacy other than the one that made the partial fill.
decision_logic.action: Decline: Massachusetts keeps the remainder at the original pharmacy, and no federal transfer pathway reaches a partially filled prescription.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts written or electronic Schedule II prescription is presented for its first dispensing, partial or full.
decision_logic.action: Count from the day after it was written as day one; past day 30 it is invalid under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) and nothing may be dispensed on it.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule II opioid prescription lacks the s. 22(c) notation and the patient asks for a lesser quantity.
decision_logic.action: Do not refuse her request and do not fill in full over it; contact the prescriber to cure the omission, because the federal permission requires a prescription written in accordance with State law, then dispense the lesser quantity.

decision_logic.condition: A refill question names Schedule III, IV, or Massachusetts Schedule V.
decision_logic.action: Choose the rule with the correct schedule scope, check both count and issue-date limits, and for the Massachusetts Schedule V rule confirm that the facility is not an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy.

The same-pharmacy result for the remaining portion is shared: Massachusetts states it in s. 18(d3/4), and federal law provides no transfer pathway for a partially filled prescription.
Partial-fill records are cumulative: the federal notation and dispensing record under 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(5)(ii) run alongside the Massachusetts patient-record notation.

Massachusetts limits the life of a written or electronic Schedule II prescription to 30 days from issuance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a); the federal remainder clock in 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) times only the remaining portions.

The similar five-refill and six-month formulations for Schedule III-IV and Massachusetts Schedule V must be matched to the correct schedule and facility scope; 247 CMR 9.04(13) does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

exceptions.text: A nearby rule with a familiar number is not controlling unless its actor, schedule, and triggering facts match the transaction.

Massachusetts excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from the Schedule V refill provision in 247 CMR 9.04(13), so the matching federal and state numbers do not eliminate the facility-scope inquiry. The same provision, 247 CMR 9.04(15), also disapplies the day-counting rule in 247 CMR 9.04(10) at that facility type.

The 30-day request-based remainder period is displaced by the federal 72-hour period for an emergency oral Schedule II prescription and is preceded by the Massachusetts five-day initial-dispensing limit for the s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) pathways.

Federal law still allows a one-time transfer of an electronic Schedule II prescription that has not been dispensed, for its initial dispensing; what no federal pathway reaches is the remaining portion of a partially filled one.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than 30 days after the prescription was written (federal) and not later than 30 days after the issue date (Massachusetts)
timing_deadlines.consequence: Both limits must be satisfied, and only the pharmacy that made the partial fill may dispense the remainder.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than day 30 after issuance, counting the day after the prescription was written as day one
timing_deadlines.consequence: After that the prescription is invalid under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a), and a federal clock cannot revive it.

timing_deadlines.consequence: The applicable five-refill limit must also remain unexhausted.

Massachusetts also requires each partial dispensing and its quantity to be noted in the patient's record maintained by the pharmacy, accessible to the prescribing practitioner on request; it adds to the federal records rather than replacing them.

The prescribing practitioner must include on a Massachusetts Schedule II opioid prescription a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity.

Make the federal notation for each patient-requested partial fill (who asked, on what date, and the quantity dispensed) and see that the Massachusetts notation of each partial dispensing and its quantity goes into the patient's record; the pharmacy keeps the federal dispensing record for each partial filling.

common_traps.text: Stopping after finding a permissive federal rule can omit a Massachusetts condition that still governs the dispensing.
Transplanting a correct number from the wrong schedule produces a wrong result even when the number looks familiar.
Restating the federal not-prohibited-by-State-law condition as a requirement that State law affirmatively permit the partial fill changes the default for a silent jurisdiction.
Treating a federal clock that answers 'by when' as though it also answered 'where' sends the remaining portion to a pharmacy that neither sovereign allows to dispense it.
Keeping only the Massachusetts patient-record notation omits the federal notation and dispensing record that every patient-requested partial fill also requires.

Listing only three federal partial-fill conditions drops the one a state-law defect in the prescription engages: that it be written and filled in accordance with State law.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Schedule II prescription may be partially filled at the patient or prescriber request when state law permits, with the remaining portion dispensed no later than 30 days after the prescription was written unless a shorter applicable limit controls.

authority.name: Request-based partial filling, conditions and records

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.13(a) the stock-shortage partial fill is permissible only if the pharmacist MAKES A NOTATION OF THE QUANTITY SUPPLIED on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic prescription record. The REQUEST-BASED pathway in 1306.13(b) allocates duties to both actors. Its general conditions in (b)(1) are conjunctive: the partial fill is not prohibited by State law; the prescription is written and filled in accordance with the Act, the chapter and State law; the partial fill is requested by the PATIENT, by one acting on the patient's behalf (a parent or legal guardian of a minor, or a caregiver of an adult patient named in a medical power of attorney), or by the PRACTITIONER who wrote the prescription; and THE TOTAL QUANTITY DISPENSED IN ALL PARTIAL FILLINGS DOES NOT EXCEED THE TOTAL QUANTITY PRESCRIBED. Under (b)(3), a practitioner who wants the prescription partially filled MUST SPECIFY THE QUANTITY TO BE DISPENSED IN EACH PARTIAL FILLING on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic record; after consultation with a pharmacist the practitioner may authorize a partial fill at a later date, but the prescription must still be filled not later than 30 days after it was written, or 72 hours for an emergency oral prescription. Under (b)(4) a request may be made in person, in writing if signed by the requester, or by telephone; and WHERE THE PRACTITIONER HAS ALREADY SPECIFIED QUANTITIES UNDER (b)(3), the patient, guardian or named caregiver MAY NOT REQUEST A PARTIAL FILLING GREATER THAN THE AMOUNT THE PRACTITIONER SPECIFIED. Under (b)(5) the pharmacist's notation differs by requester: a practitioner request made in consultation is noted as 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' with the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials, while a patient, guardian or caregiver request is noted as that named person having requested the partial fill on a stated date, together with the quantity dispensed. Every request-based partial filling also generates a dispensing record carrying the date, the name or initials of the dispenser, and the other elements 21 CFR 1306.22(c) requires for Schedule III and IV refills; for electronic prescriptions that information must be LINKED to the electronic prescription record.
exceptions: The stock-shortage notation under 1306.13(a) is only the quantity supplied; the fuller request-based notations belong to 1306.13(b)(5).
A consultation-authorized partial fill adds the 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' notation that a partial fill specified on the face of the prescription does not require.
Where the practitioner has specified per-fill quantities, a patient-side request cannot exceed them.
The remaining-portion period is 30 days from writing, except 72 hours where the prescription was an emergency oral one.
